title: The kidney stone
hookLine: in constant pain from stones, he writes about bearing illness (Essays 2.37)

lines: A PAIN THAT KEEPS COMING BACK.
cards: What do you do with a pain that keeps coming back? Not one bad afternoon: a pain that arrives without warning, leaves, and returns when it pleases. Montaigne lived with one.

He called it the stone, kidney stones, an illness he says he had dreaded long before it found him. In book two, chapter thirty-seven, the essay on how children resemble their fathers, he writes about living with it.
Not as a saint, not as a doctor. As a patient, a little annoyed, a little curious, and still at his desk.

teach.b: First, where it came from. His father had the stone too, Montaigne says, and he can't get over it. How could a tiny drop of seed carry the print of his father's illness, long before it ever showed?
He doesn't pretend to know. It's the same shrug as what do I know, turned on his own body.
Second, groan if you have to. He doesn't demand a brave face. If the body finds some relief in complaining, he writes, more or less, let it complain.
What he guards is his judgment: that between the attacks he still thinks his own thoughts. The face can wince. The mind stays his.

teach.h: DOUBTING THE DOCTORS OF HIS DAY.
teach.b: Third, the doctors. Much of the essay pokes fun at the medicine of his day: remedies that contradict each other, confident cures that don't cure.
Hear that as a man of his time on the medicine of his time, not as advice about yours. His point is about being too sure, not about refusing help. Fourth, patience.
He treats the stone almost like a stubborn houseguest: it comes, it goes, and he learns its habits. He even says the illness has been getting him used to the thought of dying, a little at a time.
That isn't cheerful, but it's honest, and there's a steadiness in it. Patience with pain doesn't mean liking it.
It means not adding a second fight, against the fact that it's there, on top of the first.
Whatever the pain, let the body say ouch, and keep the mind your own.

how: Readers of Montaigne often turn to his pages on the stone as a picture of living with chronic pain: letting the body complain while keeping one's judgment steady.

o: a gallstone his doctors cured with a well-known remedy
a heavy stone Montaigne kept on his desk to write by
Montaigne's painful illness, which he bore with patience

games.q: the stone essay: tap the pairs.

s: Montaigne says a person in pain must never groan
he lets the body complain if it brings relief; what he guards is his judgment.
he wonders how his father's illness could pass to him
he marvels that a tiny drop of seed could carry it, and admits he doesn't know.
he praises the doctors of his day as nearly always right
much of the essay pokes fun at the medicine of his time and its confident cures.

games.q: you're Montaigne, and the stone has come back. what do you ask of yourself?
o: a calm face, no matter what.
let the body complain, keep the mind steady.
games.why: he doesn't demand a brave face. the body may groan; what he protects is his own judgment between the attacks.

practice: Find one place that aches, or one worry that hurts like an ache, and let it be exactly the size it is: don't push it away, and don't make it bigger. If you want to sigh, sigh.
Then notice what is still yours around it: the breath, the room, the next quiet thought.

wordCard.voice: The kidney stone. Montaigne's unwelcome companion: let the body groan, and keep the mind your own. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: patient with pain. A week that began with a fall from a horse ran through books, cruelty, what do I know and the cat, to his faults and now the stone. That's the week.

sources.ref: Montaigne, Essays 2.37, Of the resemblance of children to fathers (his stone; his father's stone and the drop of seed; letting the body complain; his doubts about the medicine of his day; the illness accustoming him to death)
